title: Railway history: PGE, BCR and BC Rail
intro: Pacific Great Eastern, British Columbia Railway and BC Rail through their logos, corporate changes and railway connections. Design groups are ordered by their earliest documented use; several were used at the same time.
overview: The legal corporation, the railway’s public name, its operating subsidiary and its graphics have related histories with different dates. The visual groups above retain overlapping corporate, equipment, passenger and advertising designs. These events and connections explain the organizations behind them. Source reproductions, original photographs and currently missing masters are identified separately.

eras.label: Point Ellice diamond monogram
eras.note: The tall diamond appears on the steam tug Point Ellice; related stencils were found at Williams Lake. Kennelly cites a photograph dated 19 September 1929 and reports use into the early 1950s. Don Davis is a recollected designer attribution, not a verified credit.

applicability.note: The 1929 photograph dates documented use. It does not establish when the design was created; the artwork below is the 1991 article reproduction.

sources.title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
sources.locator: PDF page 5; historical account published January 1991

eras.label: Square diamond equipment marks
eras.note: A second, squarer diamond family had unshaded and shaded versions. The article associates the first with steam crane 6071 and the shaded version with refrigerator cars, with related examples on Combination Coach 16.

applicability.note: Around 1934 is the author’s reported introduction; February 1935 photographs attest the shaded refrigerator-car version. Later equipment sightings do not establish a universal retirement date.

sources.title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
sources.locator: PDF page 5–6; historical account published January 1991

eras.label: Circular script corporate monogram
eras.note: A script PGE monogram on passes and menus. The earliest pass Kennelly had seen was dated 1935; menus often used a single narrow circle. He found no evidence of this mark on rolling stock.

applicability.note: The first pass known to the author is evidence of use by 1935, not proof of an introduction that year.

sources.title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
sources.locator: PDF page 6; historical account published January 1991

eras.label: Early caribou equipment herald
eras.note: The early caribou appeared on new locomotives and other equipment in the second quarter of 1945. Left- and right-facing versions existed, generally facing forward on the equipment, with exceptions. The final caribou should not be credited directly to Ed Aldridge: his contest-winning submission used a landscape that the railway changed.

applicability.note: Kennelly reports the 1945 equipment introduction and the mid-1946 alteration. This is a retrospective account, not an original drawing date. The early design was phased out gradually, so mid-1946 is a revision milestone rather than a confirmed end of use.

sources.title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
sources.locator: PDF page 6–7; historical account published January 1991

eras.label: Revised caribou equipment herald
eras.note: The equipment herald was revised to a full-profile caribou and appeared in several sizes. Neck shading, chest details and proportions varied. This published illustration was traced by Kennelly from a builder photograph of Mikado 163.

applicability.note: Mid-1946 is the design change reported in the article; no month or universal withdrawal date is established.

sources.title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
sources.locator: PDF page 8; historical account published January 1991

eras.label: Corporate caribou with light lettering
eras.note: Corporate printing used a different full-profile caribou on a dark circular field. Kennelly dates its first timetable appearance to 30 September 1946. This is distinct from the equipment heralds in use at the same time.

applicability.note: The dated timetable is the first corporate appearance identified by the author. The change to bold lettering falls between the timetables of 31 May and 26 September 1948.

sources.title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
sources.locator: PDF page 7; historical account published January 1991

eras.label: Roman lettering on passenger cars
eras.note: Passenger cars gained a Roman-lettered version in 1947. The illustration records the preserved sleeping car Clinton in 1973, while the article traces the design family to sleepers acquired in 1947. It overlapped the corporate and other equipment marks.

applicability.note: The reported 1947 passenger-car introduction and the 1973 recording of this particular illustration are separate dates.

sources.title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway
sources.locator: PDF page 8; historical account published January 1991

eras.label: Corporate caribou with bold lettering
eras.note: Corporate lettering changed to bold between 31 May and 26 September 1948. Front-cover use generally ended on 7 June 1964, while back-cover use continued until the map mark appeared on 19 January 1966. The previously collected colour brochure is retained here as a related, undated print specimen; its filename is not proof of a 1955 publication date.

applicability.note: The bounded 1948 change and the later dates refer to timetable applications. They do not establish when every piece of equipment was repainted or the undated brochure was printed.

eras.label: Oval advertising caribou
eras.note: The oval accompanied the Howe Sound extension’s 1956 advertising campaign and appeared on brochures and timetables 73C and 73L. The circular corporate emblem returned by Timetable 75. The article reports no equipment use. The existing red Gateway to an Empire cover crop is a related specimen whose printing year remains uncertain.

applicability.note: 1956 dates the advertising family in Kennelly’s account, not the publication date of the undated red brochure.

eras.label: PGE and the map of British Columbia
eras.note: Kennelly dates the map mark’s replacement of the caribou on public timetables to 19 January 1966. Chuck Strawn’s archival close-up shows the equipment herald on remote-control car RCC2 around 1970. Rivets, perspective and paint texture remain visible because this is an application photograph.

applicability.note: The 1966 date applies to timetables. The archive dates its equipment photograph circa 1970; neither establishes first use of every form of the map identity.

eras.label: British Columbia Railway dogwood
eras.note: A contemporary September 1972 Canadian Rail caption calls the dogwood BCR’s new corporate symbol. The cropped artwork here is the dogwood and stacked name as reproduced in the January 1991 Cariboo masthead. The contemporaneous evidence dates the symbol family, not every detail of this later wordmark reproduction.

applicability.note: 1972 is supported for the new dogwood symbol. January 1991 is the reproduction date; this newsletter masthead does not prove the railway still used this exact lockup then.

eras.label: BC Rail operating identity
eras.note: The public BC Rail name dates to 19 June 1984. The familiar red-and-blue graphic must be dated separately: later caboose research distinguishes white lettering in 1985 and a red-and-blue herald in 1986–1987 schemes. The supporting photograph below documents the latter graphic on locomotives on 21 July 1990. A verified isolated master is still sought.

applicability.note: A name change, a claimed word-mark use date and an equipment paint scheme do not establish the first company-wide use of a particular graphic.

eras.label: The continuing BC Railway Company
eras.note: The provincial company continues after CN’s 2004 acquisition of the freight operating business. Its own website uses this BC Railway Company wordmark. It is a separate specimen from the former operating subsidiary’s BC Rail graphics.

applicability.note: The existing gallery file was collected from the official website on 22 October 2026. No design introduction date has been established.

events.description: The Howe Sound, Pemberton Valley & Northern Railway Company preceded PGE. The existing undertaking was taken over in 1912; this is an acquisition connection rather than evidence that the two legal corporations were simply the same company under different names.

events.title: Pacific Great Eastern Railway Company created
events.description: The incorporation Act establishes a new company and authorizes a line toward a junction with Grand Trunk Pacific at or near Fort George. Its railway and traffic agreement with GTP did not make PGE a demonstrated GTP subsidiary.

events.title: PGE comes under provincial ownership
events.description: After default on bond obligations, the Province became PGE’s sole owner and shareholder. The company’s 1912 incorporation and the beginning of its Crown ownership are separate milestones.

events.title: A landscape submission becomes a caribou identity
events.description: Ed Aldridge won the railway’s logo competition with a landscape and motto. Kennelly cites a letter of 15 June 1945 saying the central image had been changed to a caribou. The dinner-plate scene shown below is not Aldridge’s original submission; its connection to the unused idea is Kennelly’s suggestion.

sources.title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway

events.title: PGE reaches Prince George
events.description: PGE’s north–south route finally reached Prince George in 1952. The east–west Grand Trunk Pacific route had reached the city in 1914 and later formed part of CN. These were distinct railway lines meeting in the same city.

sources.title: Central BC Railway and Forestry Museum — History
sources.locator: Opening historical paragraph

events.title: Howe Sound extension accompanies a new advertising mark
events.description: Kennelly connects completion of the Howe Sound extension with the oval caribou advertising campaign. This was a specialized advertising variant rather than a universal replacement of the circular equipment and corporate emblems.

sources.title: The Cariboo, Issue Three, January 1991; Greg M. Kennelly, Logos of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway

events.title: PGE becomes British Columbia Railway Company
events.description: The one-page Act changes the name of the existing corporation while preserving its rights, liabilities and property. This is corporate continuity, not the creation of a separate successor company.

events.title: British Columbia Railway and the dogwood
events.description: Contemporary reporting gives 1 April as the public name-change date and calls the dogwood the railway’s new corporate symbol. The public rollout is recorded separately from the statute’s 30 March assent.

events.title: Harbours Board railway assets pass to BCR
events.description: The Auditor General records the railway assets transferring to BCR effective 31 October 1983; other Harbours Board assets went to BC Development Corporation. Asset transfer and the Board’s later legal dissolution are separate events.

events.title: Rail operations and property move into subsidiaries
events.description: BCR Properties was incorporated on 18 May. S.C. Holdings was renamed BC Rail Ltd. on 28 May, and the group transferred assets into its railway and property subsidiaries on 12 June. British Columbia Railway Company remained the parent.

events.description: The centenary history dates adoption of the shorter BC Rail name to 19 June. CIPO’s later word-mark application claims services use from 18 May 1984, a different kind of evidence. Neither record establishes the introduction date of every red-and-blue graphic variant.

events.title: BCR Partnership established
events.description: A further restructuring put substantially all of the railway assets into BCR Partnership. The subsidiary and partnership structure helps explain the interests transferred to CN in 2004.

events.title: CN acquires the freight operating business
events.description: The transaction transferred BC Rail Ltd. shares and BCR Partnership units to CN, together with rights to operate freight services over publicly owned railway infrastructure. The continuing provincial company was not dissolved or renamed CN. The TSB’s history uses 15 July for the system’s operational transition; this is kept separate from the government’s 14 July legal closing.

events.description: British Columbia Railway Company became a wholly owned subsidiary of the BC Transportation Financing Authority. The ownership hierarchy changed while the statutory railway company continued.

events.description: The audited statements record the retained railway right-of-way and infrastructure leased to CN, the Port Subdivision serving Roberts Bank, and property activities through BCR Properties. These surviving interests explain why the present company still has its own identity.

evidence.label: PGE dinner-plate landscape decoration
evidence.caption: The printed dinner-plate scene is decorative context, not an adopted PGE logo and not the original contest submission. Kennelly suggests a possible connection to Aldridge’s unused landscape idea; that connection remains attributed to the author.
evidence.sourceLocator: The Cariboo, Issue 3, January 1991, PDF page 6

evidence.caption: MLW RS-3, road class RS-16, numbers 561–578; dimensions taken from unit 571. Black-and-white coded drawing, not a colour image. LG=light green; DG=dark green; Y=yellow; B=black. Source says not all units appeared in this scheme. Map herald and numbers shown at cab; exact logo artwork is too small to use as a clean master. Greg M.
